label: Run 13 · Ali Wong
note: Written by Ali Wong from what they wrote about the two characters, improvisation by improvisation (run 13: run 12 with the turn no longer fixed at one message from each). Before each of the 11 improvisations the writer was told how it goes for Reuben_404: the approach taken, how well it comes off, how it goes wrong on a miss, any trap (a way of going wrong that carries on into the next improvisations: Spiral, Overthinking, Fixation and the rest) and how the other's interest moves. IMPROVISATIONS holds each instruction and what the writer wrote for it. The instructions are part of the design and stay. Score the chat as the reader gets it, the bar unchanged, but read each part against what was asked: where a score comes from what an instruction asked for (a fumble, a trap, interest lost or won), its cause is the improvisation; where the writer carried an instruction out badly, or the weakness has nothing to do with the instructions, it is the writing. The reader sees no dice and no plan: where a dimension speaks of turns, read improvisations.

chat.test.why: The reader gets all four for both characters right. Reuben fears being seen and looked away from. He covers it with narration and getting his flaws in first, and it traces to Delphine and the 'watch something' girl. Brick fears that 'sometime' means never. She covers it with scheduling and threatening to revoke first, and it traces to Marguerite and the cab. Both endings come out of those fears: Reuben's 'zero commentary, coat on' and Brick's '00:15 locked' are each the fear answered. It stops short of a 6 because Reuben's fear reaches the reader only as a flat statement, so it is told rather than understood. Brick's poorer past (microwaved pigs-in-a-blanket, heels over couches) never connects to her control, so the reader says her scheduling's origin 'is not in the chat.'
evidence: if i stop tap-dancing for ten seconds you'll see a crooked four-inch shut-in and politely look away
"Sometime" is just "never" for cowards. You're losing your 23:41.

chat.test.raise: Let Reuben's fear show only through Brick catching it, not through his own sentence, and tie Brick's pigs-in-a-blanket childhood to why she needs the clock.

The empty studio is also explained on request. What does come out sideways is minor. The 'thumb slipped' line gives away his eagerness. In Turn 7 the 'definitely not judging' denial lets the 11-day shut-in leak out, and that is the one real slip. It is not a 3 because nothing that matters is found out: the reader is told it.

chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest moment is Reuben's last line: "invite accepted, coat on, zero commentary. let's go split a security deposit on those empty floorboards." All chat long he can't stop narrating himself with parentheticals, "aaand i'm narrating my own unmatch again," and play-by-play, and Brick keeps naming it as the problem. This line has no aside. It even announces "zero commentary" and then honors it. It also brings back his opening joke about Victorian landlords splitting a security deposit, but sincerely this time, as a plan. Brick's reply ("00:15 locked") treats it as accepted, which suggests she read it as genuine too.

The line just before it is a near miss: "i'm never giving you 'sometime.' i'm booking your 00:15 tonight, your Tuesday at 19:00, and every Sunday after that in permanent ink (okay, that one actually felt really good to type)." The commitment answers her real wound, the cab guy's "sometime," directly. But he still tacks on a parenthetical. The aside itself is unusually candid, though. It reports a feeling rather than scoring himself as a comeback ("buzzer-beater, i'm back in"). So it's partway out of the act.

For Brick, the strongest candidate is her explanation of why she hates "let's just vibe": "My ex Marguerite dumped me for putting our fights on a shared calendar with hard stop-times, and the next guy said 'let's do this again sometime' in a cab and left me sobbing in traffic." Until then she speaks in clipped, mock-bureaucratic commands ("You have my 23:30–23:40 slot. Proceed."). Here she gives names, admits she was dumped, and offers an image of herself crying in traffic, which cuts against her controlled persona. She recovers the act immediately ("You're losing your 23:41"). Her "...My monocle just fogged" line shows a similar crack. The ellipsis and "Don't tease... unless you're actually going to hold me to it" read as a real request, though she's still wearing the costume.

Reuben's "if i stop tap-dancing for ten seconds you'll see a crooked four-inch shut-in and politely look away" states his fear plainly. But by his own framing it's still him "typing out my own obituary," so the performance hasn't stopped yet.

The text only gives me their words, so "how I could tell" rests on these shifts: dropped asides, personal specifics, and the other person's response. Whether either of them actually felt unguarded isn't something the chat itself can confirm.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben_404**

**What he fears:** Being seen as he is when he stops performing. He says it outright: "if i stop tap-dancing for ten seconds you'll see a crooked four-inch shut-in and politely look away." The fear peaks when things go well: "right on cue i'm tanking this chat in real time because you actually said yes."

**What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:** He narrates himself constantly, through meta-asides and parentheses: "(okay, that landed, i'm somehow clawing this chat back from the grave)," "aaand i'm narrating my own unmatch again," "(holy shit, buzzer-beater, i'm back in)." He also gets ahead of judgment by disclosing first: "i'll save your lens the audit—4.5 inches, forty-degree left hook." And he presents a looser self than he lives. He claims "i'm barely ever in my apartment, i thrive on not knowing what's happening next," then admits to "a freezing flat i haven't left in 11 days." Brick names the pattern: "You are actively filibustering your own erection."

**Where it comes from:** He points to two past relationships. "my ex Delphine left because i couldn't say one un-performed sentence, and the girl after her said 'we can just watch something' when my left hook caught wrong on re-entry." The chat doesn't say whether the habit started before Delphine. Her leaving because of it suggests it already existed.

**What he did at the end:** He commits and drops the commentary. "i'm never giving you 'sometime.'" That line still has a parenthesis, but the aside is sincere: "(okay, that one actually felt really good to type)." His last line has none: "invite accepted, coat on, zero commentary." For someone who hasn't left in 11 days, "coat on" means he is leaving the flat. Whether he actually arrives is not in the chat.

**Brick_haus**

**What he fears:** Vague promises that turn into being left. "'Sometime' is just 'never' for cowards." He fears being let down when he hopes: "Don't tease a timestamped itinerary with buffers unless you're actually going to hold me to it."

**What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:** He schedules everything and controls the terms. "You have my 23:30–23:40 slot." "23:41 is allocated for estate rosé." He keeps threatening to withdraw before he can be left: "You're losing your 23:41," "sixty seconds before your slot expires and I revoke your calendar access permanently," "One more meta-aside and I'm eating my microwaved pigs-in-a-blanket alone." He also cleared out what reminded him of the past: "I threw out every chair Marguerite ever touched."

**Where it comes from:** Two incidents. "My ex Marguerite dumped me for putting our fights on a shared calendar with hard stop-times." Then "the next guy said 'let's do this again sometime' in a cab and left me sobbing in traffic." The cab guy explains his hatred of "sometime." The scheduling habit itself predates Marguerite, since it is why she left, and its origin is not in the chat.

**What he did at the end:** He bends his own rules and commits, still in his calendar language. "Fine. 23:40 extended." "00:15 locked." He keeps a playful threat ("I'm confiscating the top hat") but no longer threatens to end things. Whether the meeting happens is not in the chat.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
I'd have stopped at Reuben's "you literally just said no more meta-asides and here i am typing out my own obituary…" line, or at the latest at Brick's "It is 23:39. You have sixty seconds…" reply.

The first third earns attention. The opening is quick and odd, with the Victorian landlords, the pre-emptive audit, and the Helvetica Bold vein. Reuben's claim that he's a "no plans, let's just vibe" guy who's "barely ever in my apartment" quietly sets up a lie for later. Brick's reveal about Marguerite and the cab guy gives the scheduling bit a wound underneath it. Reuben's answer, "00:40 scheduled fight with a hard stop so nobody ever leaves," is the best line in the piece, because it turns Brick's neurosis into an act of care. Brick's "My monocle just fogged" lands as a real shift.

After that the chat settles into one loop and repeats it. Reuben narrates his own collapse, Brick scolds him, and Reuben narrates the scolding. By my count that happens about five times:

* "tanking this chat in real time"
* "(okay, that landed…)"
* "aaand i'm narrating my own unmatch again"
* "here i am typing out my own obituary"
* "(holy shit, buzzer-beater…)"

Brick's rebukes escalate in wording but not in kind. The new information that arrives during the loop (Delphine, the 11-day shut-in, the ring light, the £84.99 pump) is good, but it's delivered in the same register, so it reads like more of the same joke. Once Brick names the pattern outright ("panicked sports broadcaster"), the reader has the whole mechanism. Everything after that is waiting for the resolution.

There are a few points where I could predict exactly what came next:

* **"One more meta-aside and I'm eating my microwaved pigs-in-a-blanket alone."** This rule exists to be broken, so Reuben's next message will be a meta-aside, and the date will survive anyway.
* **"You have sixty seconds."** A countdown in a chat like this guarantees a last-second save. It also guarantees Reuben slips once more during the save and Brick forgives him. Both happen.
* **The cab guy's "sometime."** Once that's established as the wound, the romantic climax was always going to be Reuben swearing off "sometime" and booking concrete times. "I'm never giving you 'sometime'" arrives right on schedule.
* **The final two messages.** With top hat, security deposit, left hook, and audit all planted in the first four lines, the closing exchange was going to be a callback round. I expected the security deposit and the audit specifically, and got both.

Things I didn't see coming include the cab-sobbing detail, the "fight with a hard stop so nobody ever leaves" turn, and the plastic-tap rosé admission.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
My guess is that Reuben finally stops narrating and sends one plain, unperformed line inside the sixty seconds, and Brick_haus answers by actually sending the calendar invite.

The chat sets this up. Each of them has one wound that the other's flaw keeps hitting. Reuben's is that he "couldn't say one un-performed sentence," which is why Delphine left, and he keeps proving it with commentary on his own collapse. Brick_haus's is "sometime," the vague non-commitment that left him sobbing in a cab. The 23:39 ultimatum is engineered so that the one thing that saves the match, a single sincere sentence, is exactly what Reuben has said he can't do. The cleanest payoff is that he does it, probably as something short and concrete like confirming he'll be there at 00:15. That would also answer Brick's fear, because it's a specific commitment rather than a "sometime."

I also expect callbacks to pay off. The likeliest is the earlier joke that Brick will have to hold him down by the brim of the top hat to stop "the voice." The fight "with a hard stop so nobody ever leaves" could return too, and so could the boxed rosé and the empty studio. A last beat where Brick relaxes his own rigidity a little, perhaps by giving up the 23:41 slot, would round out the symmetry.

The other possibility is that Reuben narrates one more time and gets cut off. That would fit his self-sabotage, but the earlier "my monocle just fogged" moment shows Brick is already won over and is looking for a reason to stay. So I lean toward the warmer ending. This is a prediction from the pattern of the conversation, though. I haven't seen the actual final turn, so I can't say for certain how it lands.

chat.voices.ask: The speakers' names are hidden. Using the two characters described, say who sent each numbered message, with a few words of reason each.
chat.voices.answer:

Brick writes in capitalized, clipped sentences, uses timestamps and the language of audits and calendars, and mentions her own backstory: Marguerite, rosé, the monocle.

1. Reuben. Lowercase, and the first of a three-message burst. "23:30 sharp" sounds like Brick, but her reply in 4 calls the sender "Punctual," so she is answering it. This is the least certain one.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
Here are the recurring elements, roughly in order of first appearance.

- **Top hat and monocle.** These start as a joke about matching outfits ("two Victorian landlords"). When they come back, they mean something different each time. "Pull your top hat together" turns the hat into a stand-in for Reuben's composure. "Hold me down by the brim" makes it a handle for restraint. "My monocle just fogged" signals that Brick is moved. "Confiscating the top hat" makes it a stake or penalty. "Keep the top hat on… I need leverage" makes it a literal grip.

- **Landlords and the security deposit.** At first this is just part of the costume joke. At the end, "split a security deposit on those empty floorboards" reads as moving in, or shared commitment. The final "landlord" is now a pet name rather than a jab.

- **The audit.** Reuben opens with "I'll save your lens the audit," pre-empting judgment of his body. Brick closes with "while I audit that left hook." The scrutiny Reuben tried to head off is now welcomed and affectionate.

- **The left hook and its size.** Reuben first offers "4.5 inches, forty-degree left hook" as breezy self-disclosure. It shows up neutrally in the 00:25 itinerary. Then it turns into a wound: it "caught wrong on re-entry" with the girl after Delphine, and he calls himself a "crooked four-inch shut-in." Notice that the number shrinks as his shame grows. In "pin my crooked shaft down" he offers it rather than hides it, and Brick's final line embraces it.

- **The dorsal ridge bump.** This is Brick's self-description, and it reappears only in Reuben's itinerary. Its meaning doesn't really change; it just gets folded into the plan.

- **The schedule, slots and timestamps.** These begin as Brick's comic rigidity: the 23:30–23:40 slot, the 23:41 rosé. The Marguerite story reveals the rigidity is tied to being left. The schedule then becomes a pressure device ("It is 23:39. You have sixty seconds"). By the end, booking Tuesday and every Sunday "in permanent ink" turns scheduling into a declaration of commitment.

- **The tattoo.** "Tattooed down your shaft" starts as a joke about the schedule, with Brick's "Helvetica Bold" reply. Reuben's "permanent ink" echoes it. Brick's "I'll tattoo you onto my shaft" flips it: now Reuben would be the thing written into his life.

- **23:41 and the rosé.** At first this is something to "annex." Brick then threatens it as something Reuben is "losing." It returns deflated, as a three-litre box with a plastic tap. The chat doesn't say whether the rosé itself ever gets the slot back. Instead, the 23:40 slot gets extended.

- **"Let's just vibe" and having no plans.** This starts as Reuben's breezy persona and Brick's pet peeve. Brick's story then reframes the phrase as cowardice ("'sometime' is just 'never'"). Reuben's claim to be "barely ever in my apartment" is later contradicted by "a freezing flat I haven't left in 11 days." So the original line retroactively reads as a performance.

- **"Sometime."** This is the cab guy's wound. It comes back as Reuben's promise: "I'm never giving you 'sometime.'" A source of hurt has been turned into a vow.

- **The scheduled fight with a hard stop.** This is the habit Marguerite left Brick over. Reuben puts it into the itinerary "so nobody ever leaves," reframing the reason Brick was dumped as the thing that keeps someone around.

- **The minimalist or empty studio.** "Minimalist" first sounds like a style choice. It turns out the studio is empty because Brick threw out every chair Marguerite touched, which makes it a sign of grief. It then becomes the "empty floor" Reuben will bring his ring light to, the "floorboards" Brick will pin him to, and finally the place they'll "split a security deposit." The emptiness changes from loss to space they'll share.

- **The ring light.** This first appears as part of Reuben's embarrassing shut-in confession. It comes back as something he'll bring over, turning shame into an offering.

- **Pigs-in-a-blanket.** These start as Brick's threat to eat alone. They come back as a shared item in the itinerary and as a deadline. Loneliness has become a plan.

- **Narration, meta-asides and parentheses.** Reuben's running commentary is a defence, and the chat links it explicitly to Delphine leaving because he "couldn't say one un-performed sentence." Brick objects again and again. The parentheses keep returning: "that landed," "buzzer-beater." The last one, "okay, that one actually felt really good to type," reads as sincere rather than performed. He then closes with "zero commentary," so the habit ends either redeemed or dropped.

- **Being held down or pinned.** This begins as Reuben's half-joking plea to be physically stopped "so I can't do the voice anymore." It becomes "pin my crooked shaft down until I legally cannot speak," and then Brick's "pinned to my floorboards." It shifts from a desperate request to be silenced into mutual desire.

- **The sports-broadcaster framing.** Brick uses it as a criticism ("panicked sports broadcaster"). Reuben then adopts it knowingly with "buzzer-beater," so the same image moves from insult to self-aware joke.

- **The calendar invite and access.** It moves from "send the invite" to "revoke your calendar access" to "one calendar confirmation away" to "invite accepted." The meaning stays fairly consistent, but the stakes rise from a flirt to a threat to acceptance.

Some elements appear once and never return, such as the girth pump, the "no structure" bravado after it's undercut, and the 10-minute travel buffer apart from Brick's "hold me to it."
